meta.location: The court of king Noah, in the land of Lehi-Nephi

world_behind.title: The speech does not stop at the chapter break
world_behind.text: Verse 1 opens "after Abinadi had spoken these words he stretched forth his hand and said," which is a continuation formula. The same construction opens Mosiah 13. One sermon has been divided into four printed chapters, and the seams are all mid-argument.

world_behind.title: The gesture
world_behind.text: Stretching forth the hand appears throughout this record at the moment a speaker takes authority over a room: Ammon, Alma, Samuel on the wall, and Christ at Bountiful. Abinadi uses it to move from explaining Isaiah to charging the men in front of him.

world_behind.title: Watchmen who agree
world_behind.text: Isaiah's line about seeing eye to eye (Isa. 52:8) describes lookouts on a wall reporting the same thing at the same moment. It has already passed twice through this trial before it reaches verse 1. What the agreement is finally about, here, is that the judgments are just.

world_behind.title: The judgment furniture is legal again
world_behind.text: A bar to stand before, works weighed, a verdict with two outcomes. Chapter 15 described redemption as a settled claim. This chapter keeps the same room and changes who is standing in it.

world_behind.title: Reclassifying the law
world_behind.text: Verses 14 and 15 are addressed to men whose profession is teaching the law of Moses. Abinadi does not tell them to stop. He tells them to add one thing to the syllabus, a smaller demand than it sounds and a larger one than they can accept.

world_behind.title: A formal close
world_behind.text: The sermon ends with "Amen," the only one in the whole speech. What follows in the record is a death sentence, issued in the next verse.

world_behind.title: A judgment register borrowed from the prophets
world_behind.text: Howling, weeping, wailing, and gnashing of teeth is a stacked formula. Isaiah uses howling for cities under sentence (Isa. 13:6); the gospels pair wailing with gnashing (Matt. 13:42). Verse 2 runs all four together. Neither source does that, and it is the only place in the whole sermon where the volume goes up.

words.text: To acknowledge openly, in the older sense of conceding a fact rather than admitting a fault. What everyone concedes is that God's judgments are just. The verse describes universal agreement about the court.

Of the flesh, governed by appetite. It runs three times through verses 3 and 5, first as a description of what the fall produced, then as a nature someone can persist in. The word moves from a condition inherited to a condition chosen inside two verses.

Keeps on, refuses to leave off. The verb governs the whole exclusion: what condemns is continuing in it. Abinadi pairs it with "goes on in the ways of sin and rebellion," so both halves of the clause describe motion.

Freedom from decay, the condition of a body that will not rot. It is paired with immortality and set against corruption, and both pairs are described as clothing put on. The image is of something added to a body instead of a body exchanged.

The rail a defendant stands at in court. Treated at 2 Nephi 33:11. This record uses the phrase "the bar of God" six times across four books, and it is always a place someone is brought to. Here the bringing is done by the resurrection itself.

An outline cast by something real that has not yet arrived. Abinadi had already told these men that what they did with him would be a type and a shadow. Now he applies the same category to the law they teach, so their profession points at something beyond it.

phrases.term: Every nation, kindred, tongue, and people shall see eye to eye
phrases.text: Isaiah's two watchmen on a wall, expanded to the whole world. The formula "nation, kindred, tongue, and people" belongs to this record, so the sentence is half quotation and half Nephite idiom, joined without a visible seam.

phrases.term: That old serpent that did beguile our first parents
phrases.text: The title appears in Revelation (Rev. 12:9) and once earlier in this record, in Lehi's teaching to Jacob (2 Ne. 2:18). Abinadi uses it to explain a mechanism rather than to tell a story: the serpent is named as the cause of the fall, and the fall as the cause of a condition everybody inherits.

phrases.term: Speaking of things to come as though they had already come
phrases.text: Abinadi explaining his own grammar, and the clause occurs once in scripture. Isaiah 53, which he read out two chapters ago, describes a death in the past tense. Here he tells the court that this is deliberate and says why: the thing is settled, so it may be spoken of as done.

phrases.term: The sting of death is swallowed up in Christ
phrases.text: Paul writes almost these words to Corinth (1 Cor. 15:55), with victory where this has Christ. The substitution changes the sentence from a statement about an outcome to a statement about a person. The verse before it argued by supposing the resurrection away; this one simply asserts it.

phrases.term: He is the light and the life of the world
phrases.text: Two titles joined, and the joined form appears twice more in this record, both times spoken by Christ himself at Bountiful. Here they belong to a sentence somebody else is saying about him, roughly two centuries before he says it about himself.

phrases.term: The arms of mercy were extended towards them, and they would not
phrases.text: The refusal is stated three times over in this verse. They would not call, would not depart, would not repent, and all of it stands against a mercy described as already extended and waiting. Nothing in the verse says the arms were withdrawn.

phrases.term: Only in and through Christ ye can be saved
phrases.text: The single sentence in the chapter addressed directly to the men in the room, and it is put as a question about trembling. Everything before it is third person. Here Abinadi says "ye," and asks whether they ought not to tremble.

phrases.term: Teach them that redemption cometh through Christ the Lord
phrases.text: The last thing Abinadi says, and it is an instruction instead of a verdict. He is speaking to professional teachers, and the sentence assumes they will go on teaching. It ends with "Amen," and the next thing in the record is the order for his death.

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: The day everyone agrees
verses.text: The record has the speaker stretch forth his hand and then makes universal agreement the first item: "every nation, kindred, tongue, and people shall see eye to eye and shall confess before God that his judgments are just." The phrase "see eye to eye" is Isaiah 52:8, which the record quotes in full at 3 Nephi 20:32 in a passage about watchmen rather than about judgment. Verse 2 supplies the separation with four verbs, "howl, and weep, and wail, and gnash their teeth," and then states the ground, "because they would not hearken unto the voice of the Lord."

verses.label: v. 3–5
verses.title: Why anyone is lost
verses.text: A serpent, a fall, an inherited condition, and then a choice to remain in it. The passage is careful about the order: all mankind became carnal by the fall, and it is persisting that leaves a man "as though there was no redemption made."

verses.label: v. 6–8
verses.title: Two suppositions, then a fact
verses.text: If Christ had not come, no redemption; if he had not risen, no resurrection. Both are stated as removals to show what would collapse. Then the shortest sentence in the chapter cancels both: "But there is a resurrection."

verses.label: v. 9
verses.title: Endless, defined twice
verses.text: A light that can never be darkened and a life in which there can be no more death. Each title is explained by naming the thing that cannot happen to it, which is a plainer way of saying endless than the word itself.

verses.label: v. 10–11
verses.title: One resurrection, two destinations
verses.text: Everyone is brought to stand and judged by works. The same event delivers endless life to some and endless damnation to others, and the verse calls both of them resurrections. The sorting happens after the raising, not instead of it.

verses.label: v. 12
verses.title: They would not
verses.text: Three refusals stacked in one sentence, each with mercy already extended on the other side of it. The verse gives no account of what they wanted instead. It only records, three times, what was offered and declined.

verses.label: v. 13–15
verses.title: The assignment
verses.text: The record closes the sermon by giving the priests a teaching rule rather than a verdict: "if ye teach the law of Moses, also teach that it is a shadow of those things which are to come." The word "shadow" is doing technical work and returns in the same sense at Mosiah 3:15, "many signs, and wonders, and types, and shadows showed he unto them." Verse 15 then attaches a title that will be argued over, "Christ the Lord, who is the very Eternal Father," which is the identification the priests dispute at Mosiah 7:27. The last thing said to the court is an instruction about how to keep teaching, delivered by a man they are about to burn.

chapter.title: Abinadi explains his own grammar
chapter.text: Verse 6 names the convention he has been using: things to come spoken of as though they had already come. The clause occurs once in scripture, and it arrives two chapters after he read out an entire prophecy in the past tense. He does not defend the practice. He states it and moves on.

chapter.title: "See eye to eye" has now travelled three times
chapter.text: A priest quoted it out of Isaiah 52 to open the trial; Abinadi recited it back at the close of his exposition; and now he says who will do the seeing. The same six words are used to ask a question, to answer it, and to apply it.

chapter.title: The shortest sentence carries the turn
chapter.text: "But there is a resurrection." Four words, after two verses of supposing the opposite, and the rest of the chapter follows from it. Abinadi spends more words removing the resurrection hypothetically than asserting it.

chapter.title: The chapter is a charge
chapter.text: Chapter 15 explained who the servant was. This one draws the consequence and hands out instructions. The move from third person to "ye" happens at verse 13 and does not go back.

chapter.title: The exclusion rests on continuing
chapter.text: Verses 3 through 5 establish that everyone became carnal, then locate the problem in persisting. Verse 12 makes the same distinction with verbs of refusal. Nothing in the chapter condemns anyone for the inherited condition it spends three verses describing.

chapter.title: Corinthians vocabulary in a Nephite courtroom
chapter.text: Sting, victory, mortal putting on immortality, corruption putting on incorruption. The terms track 1 Corinthians 15 closely enough to notice, in a sermon set roughly two centuries before Paul.

chapter.title: It ends by assuming they keep their jobs
chapter.text: The last instruction is about how to teach the law of Moses, addressed to the men about to condemn him. He does not tell them to resign or repent of teaching. He tells them what to add.

chapter.title: Role in the unit
chapter.text: The trial runs Mosiah 11 through 17: the charge, the law, Isaiah, the exposition, this closing argument, and the fire. Mosiah 17:1 opens "when Abinadi had finished these sayings," which makes verse 15 the last thing he said before the sentence.

applications.title: Say when you are speaking as if it were done
applications.text: Abinadi flagged his own convention before it could confuse anyone. When you speak about something certain but not yet actual, saying so costs one sentence and prevents a lot of misunderstanding.

applications.title: Locate the problem in the persisting
applications.text: The chapter does not condemn the condition everyone inherited; it condemns going on in it. Ask whether what you are carrying is something you received or something you are actively continuing.

applications.title: Notice a mercy that is already extended
applications.text: The verse records what was offered and declined, three times over, and never says the offer closed. If you are waiting for an opening, check whether it has been open the whole time.

applications.title: Argue by removal when assertion is not landing
applications.text: Suppose the thing away and describe what collapses. It is often easier to see what something is doing by taking it out than by praising it.

applications.title: Add rather than demand a resignation
applications.text: Abinadi told teachers of the law to keep teaching and to add one thing. When someone's whole practice looks wrong to you, consider whether a single addition would reorder it.

applications.title: Define by what cannot happen to it
applications.text: Verse 9 explains two large words by naming the thing each one rules out. When a term has gone vague from use, try saying what it excludes rather than what it includes.

applications.title: Ask whether you tremble
applications.text: The one direct question in the chapter is not about belief. It asks whether the situation described has produced any reaction at all in the people hearing it.

questions.text: What would I concede is just if I could see the whole of it?
What am I persisting in and calling a nature?
If I were judged by works today, which ones would I want counted?
What has been extended toward me that I have not called on?
What am I treating as the destination that was meant to be a pointer?
If I had one sentence left, what would I tell people to teach?
